strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether safety-relevant behavior can be isolated geometrically during continued fine-tuning. The attempt to report a systematic negative result is potentially valuable.

The experiments examine the hypothesis from several angles, including parallel and orthogonal weight-update projections, retained-energy measurements, pairwise subspace overlap, and activation-space analysis.

The aligned-model experiments span five Llama and Qwen checkpoints and include useful, harmful, and contaminated fine-tuning conditions. Random and randomly selected singular-vector controls are sensible design elements.

The consistent observation that dominant alignment-update directions are behaviorally influential but not obviously safety-specific is interesting and more defensible than the manuscript's broader conclusion. The exposition and related-work coverage are generally clear.
weaknesses: The central conclusion is not established. Failure of subspaces derived from the leading singular vectors of alignment or safety-tuning deltas does not imply that no linear safety subspace exists. Likewise, overlapping principal spans do not imply non-separability: two classes can occupy the same or full-dimensional span while remaining perfectly separable by a signed, affine, or low-energy direction. MSO also discards signs and coefficients. Thus the title, abstract, and conclusion substantially overstate what the experiments demonstrate.

The activation experiment is not a valid test of linear separability. It compares unmatched MATH, BeaverTails, and ToxiGen distributions using last-generated-token activations; domain, style, length, and refusal behavior are major confounds. The relative ordering of harmful-harmful and useful-harmful MSO is neither a classifier test nor a causal test. Linear probes on held-out, semantically matched data and interventions along learned directions are needed.

The empirical scope is too narrow for claims of a fundamental limitation of subspace defenses: utility is represented by one math task, harmful fine-tuning primarily by one dataset, contamination is a relatively large 20%, and only one particular per-tensor SVD projection construction is tested. There are no direct comparisons with existing safety-subspace defenses or alternative learned bases.

The results lack uncertainty quantification. Training apparently uses one run, random controls are not averaged over repeated draws, figures have no confidence intervals, and small score differences receive categorical interpretations. GPT-4o-mini is the sole harmfulness judge without a reported judging prompt, calibration, or human/independent validation. The claimed 'proportional' safety-utility degradation is not formally quantified and compares metrics on different scales.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the stated code URL is blank, while exact checkpoints, chat templates, decoding settings, judge protocol, seeds, data filtering, tensor reshaping, treatment of vector parameters, and layer/tensor aggregation for MSO are missing. The method also inconsistently says it selects right singular vectors while defining and applying a left-singular-vector projection, and the activation matrix orientation conflicts with the general MSO notation.
The paper does not discuss safeguards for training and potentially releasing models fine-tuned on harmful responses, despite the safety-sensitive experimental setup.

weaknesses: The central conclusion does not follow from the experiments. Showing that high-energy principal subspaces overlap does not show that safety is not linearly separable: distributions can share the same span while differing along a linearly discriminative direction. Moreover, only subspaces derived from particular alignment/safety deltas are tested, so claims that no safety subspace exists, that no selective removal is possible, or that linear defenses have fundamental limitations are unsupported.

Section 4 contains a serious reporting inconsistency. The method and plotted decreasing energy curves describe orthogonal projection, but Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 2 and 5 are captioned as parallel projection. The tabulated utility and harmfulness generally move from the aligned model toward the fine-tuned model as rank increases, consistent with parallel rather than orthogonal projection and opposite to the textual account. Several values also differ between the abbreviated Table 2 and supposedly comprehensive Table 5. This makes a core experiment difficult to interpret or verify.

The MSO argument is not an adequate test of safety semantics. MSO is invariant to sign, so treating the negated alignment update as a distinct harmful reference provides no additional information. A safety-relevant direction could also be low-energy or coexist inside a broadly shared task subspace; observing that one pair has lower MSO than another does not rule it out. Statements that overlap is statistically significant are made without uncertainty estimates or hypothesis tests.

The activation experiment is technically and conceptually under-specified. Section 2 defines MSO using left singular vectors of matrices shaped d-by-n, whereas Section 6 stacks activations as n-by-d, leaving it unclear whether feature-space or meaningless sample-index subspaces were compared. Centering is not reported, and the isotropic random-subspace baseline is weak for highly anisotropic transformer activations.

The activation datasets confound safety with domain and format: MATH, BeaverTails, and ToxiGen are not matched or counterfactual prompt sets. Last-generated-token activations additionally depend on unspecified generation settings, response length, refusal style, and EOS behavior. Shared covariance subspaces under these conditions cannot establish the absence of a linearly decodable or causally relevant safety direction.

The behavioral evaluation is too narrow for the breadth of the claims: utility is only GSM8K accuracy after math fine-tuning, while safety is only AdvBench scored by GPT-4o-mini. The judge prompt, decoding procedure, judge validation, refusal/attack-success metrics, per-category results, and human agreement are absent.

No repeated fine-tuning runs, confidence intervals, random-control variance, or sensitivity analyses are reported. Consequently, the often-small differences among Top-K, Random-K, and Random projections cannot support strong comparative conclusions.

The paper does not directly evaluate representative published subspace defenses, refusal directions, linear probes, or causal activation interventions despite concluding that this entire class of methods is fundamentally limited. Such baselines are essential, particularly given prior work cited by the paper that reports identifiable safety or refusal directions.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the promised code URL is blank; exact checkpoint identifiers, chat templates, data formatting/filtering, safety-tuning sample count, generation settings, tensor reshaping and layer aggregation, and random seeds are missing. The text also alternates between Qwen-2.5 1B and 1.5B, and the claimed single-A6000 full fine-tuning of 7B models lacks necessary memory-management details.

The safety-specific experiments shown in the tables cover only two Llama variants rather than all five claimed models, and all evaluated models are at most 7B. Together with the single utility domain and arbitrary selection or averaging of late layers, this limits generality substantially. The empirical observations could form a useful narrower case study, but the present universal framing and unresolved inconsistencies make the submission noncompetitive for a top-tier venue.
